awd_titl_txt: Conference: 2025 Great Plains Operator Theory Symposium
awd_abstract_narration:
This NSF award will support US-based participants to attend the 2025 edition of the Great Plains Operator Theory Symposium (GPOTS), to be held at the University of Puerto Rico – Rio Piedras, May 19-23, 2025.  GPOTS is a major international conference series on operator theory and operator algebras which is widely attended each year by mathematicians at all career stages from around the world. The 2025 edition of the conference will feature both invited and contributed talks on a wide variety of topics in these areas; participants will discuss important new developments and propose problems for future research.  More information about the meeting can be found on the conference website http://math.uprrp.edu/gpots-2025
 
GPOTS focuses on recent developments in operator algebras and operator theory, including the structure theory of C*-algebras and von Neumann algebras, free probability, noncommutative geometry, and the theory of operator spaces.  These areas of mathematics have a distinguished history in the field of analysis, and admit deep applications to many other mathematical fields, such as differential geometry, quantum information theory, dynamical systems, and mathematical physics.  The conference will provide a stimulating environment for collaboration and communication between participants.  Plenary speakers will showcase the latest trends and advancements in the field, and several sessions of contributed talks will offer participants at all career stages the opportunity to promote their own research and network with colleagues.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
$C^*$-algebras are algebras of bounded operators on a Hilbert space that are closed under the adjoint operation and the operator norm topology. Among these, the $C^*$-algebras closed under the strong operator topology are known as von Neumann algebras. A primary original motivation for the theory of von Neumann algebras was to establish a mathematically rigorous framework for the matrix mechanics model of quantum physics—a theme that remains central to the subject. Notably, the last few decades have witnessed deep connections emerging between operator algebras and quantum information theory.
By the Gelfand-Naimark theorem, the study of a locally compact Hausdorff space $X$ is equivalent to the study of the commutative $C^*$-algebra $C_0(X)$ consisting of continuous functions on $X$ vanishing at infinity. Building on this framework, Alain Connes realized that complex geometric objects—such as leaf spaces of foliations and quotient spaces of group actions on topological spaces—can be effectively studied via non-commutative $C^*$-algebras and their dense subalgebras.
In index theory, elliptic differential operators on a compact manifold are Fredholm operators. The celebrated Atiyah-Singer Index Theorem computes the Fredholm index of such an operator purely in terms of topological invariants derived from its symbol. The higher index theory of elliptic differential operators broadly generalizes this classic result, encoding structural information about global symmetries of the underlying manifold through its fundamental group. In particular, higher index theory provides a powerful framework for studying the Novikov Conjecture regarding the homotopy invariance of higher signatures on compact manifolds. Among all operator algebras, simple $C^*$-algebras are often viewed as non-commutative analogs of a single-point space. Consequently, they play a foundational role akin to elementary particles in physics or simple groups in algebra.
Recently, the classification program for simple nuclear $C^*$-algebras—commonly known as the Elliott Program—achieved a major breakthrough. A milestone theorem by Gong and Lin (building on earlier foundational work by Elliott, Gong, Lin, Niu, and others) classified all simple, separable, nuclear $C^*$-algebras of finite nuclear dimension, contingent on the Universal Coefficient Theorem (UCT) in $KK$-theory. With the simple case largely settled, structural research has increasingly shifted toward non-simple $C^*$-algebras, with a particular focus on those of real rank zero.
The lectures delivered by the keynote speakers highlighted recent breakthroughs across $C^*$-algebra classification, non-commutative geometry, quantum mathematics, and operator theory, in particular semigroups of operators. Several talks bridged fundamental quantum theory with operator algebras, emphasizing key intersections with the rapidly developing field of quantum computation.

Semigroups of linear operators in Banach constitute give a  branch of operator theory with strong connections to quantum mechanics. This relates mostly to Schr\"odinger operators. More generally, they are a convenient way to solve partial differential equations of evolution and derive their qualitative properties. The fundamental result of M. H. Stone established in 1932 on  the generators of strongly continuous unitary  groups in Hilbert space led to the the characterization of the generators of $C_0-$semigroups in Banach spaces in 1948. Extensions of the theory  include positive semigroups in Banach lattices, semigroups in Banach and $C^*$-algebras,  and nonlinear semigroups, the latter was first studied by I. E. Segal in 1963. Relevant problems concern among others the heat, wave and Schr\"odinger equations, as well as Navier-Stokes equations of fluid dynamics. This aspect of operator theory was represented at the conference where many open problems were formulated, and this will lead to collaborations among participants.%Wolfgang Arendt has contributed extensively to this area and the corresponding applications.
The conference successfully facilitated vibrant scientific exchanges among researchers spanning diverse subdisciplines and geographical regions. Providing shared lunches and coffee breaks created an informal environment that encouraged open communication and networking. This setup was especially beneficial for early-career participants—including graduate students, postdocs, and new faculty—helping integrate them into the global research community and introducing them to promising new research directions.
Crucially, the conference sparked several concrete collaborations and project outcomes:\begin{itemize}\item Jintao Deng (SUNY Buffalo) and Ryo Toyota (Texas A\&M University) initiated a joint project on the relative strong Novikov conjecture.\item Qingnan An and Zhichao Liu were inspired by Rufus Willett's lecture to solve one of Willett's open problems.\item Hang Wang connected with Huaxin Lin following Lin's lecture, leading to an ongoing collaborative research effort.\end{itemize}
